analysis.one_liner: Keeps Medicare paying doctors the old drug prices while drugmakers rebate the difference from negotiated prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 with 46 cosponsors from both parties, the bill has sat in two House committees without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, once Medicare negotiates a lower "maximum fair price" for a Part B drug (a drug given in a doctor's office, like many cancer therapies), Medicare pays the doctor the negotiated price plus 6%, which cuts into the margin community cancer clinics earn on drugs they buy. This bill flips that around: Medicare would keep paying doctors the old, higher average-sales-price payment, patients' 20% coinsurance would be figured off the lower negotiated price, and drug manufacturers would send Medicare a quarterly rebate equal to the difference. The rebates go back into the Medicare trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who receive expensive Part B drugs, especially cancer therapies, would pay less out of pocket, since their 20% coinsurance would be based on the negotiated price rather than the higher average sales price. Community oncology practices and other providers who "buy and bill" these drugs would keep the 6% add-on on the higher price, protecting revenue that current law would shrink.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare cancer patients and oncology practices

how_it_helps.text: Sets beneficiaries' coinsurance for affected negotiated drugs at 20% of a payment amount based on the negotiated maximum fair price, instead of 20% of the higher average-sales-price amount.
Restores Medicare payment for selected negotiated drugs to 106% of average sales price, the same payment doctors get for drugs that are not subject to negotiation.

Requires manufacturers to pay quarterly rebates equal to the difference between the old and negotiated payment amounts, with the money deposited into the Medicare Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, so the negotiated savings are not lost.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers pay the quarterly rebates, which under the bill's design roughly leave them at the negotiated price they would receive under current law; taxpayers are held harmless because rebates are deposited into the Medicare trust fund. The main costs are administrative: HHS must report quarterly unit and payment data and manufacturers must calculate and return rebates.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a new quarterly rebate machinery — Secretary reporting, manufacturer calculations, 30-day deadlines, and civil money penalties — where current law simply pays the negotiated price directly.
It keeps payment anchored to the higher average sales price, so the negotiated lower price reaches Medicare only through after-the-fact rebates rather than becoming the actual market price.
It preserves the 6% provider markup on the higher average sales price, a payment structure that rewards buying more expensive drugs; the savings to patients are limited to their coinsurance share.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients the bill is a real but modest win: lower coinsurance on some of the most expensive drugs in medicine. For providers it is a significant revenue protection. The cost is design, not money: instead of letting the negotiated price become the price of the drug, it maintains the higher benchmark and claws back the difference through rebates, which is more complex and leaves the 6% markup incentive intact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Murphy introduced the bill on July 7, 2025, joined by Reps. Adam Gray and Neal Dunn as original cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the standard path for Medicare drug-payment legislation, which splits jurisdiction between them.
The only actions on record since are the introduction and the dual committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.
The bill has 46 additional cosponsors, 33 Republicans and 13 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet: current law remains in place, meaning Medicare keeps negotiating lower prices and paying them directly while provider margins on those drugs shrink as negotiated prices phase in. Because the bill sits without action, neither patients nor providers nor manufacturers have seen anything change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo continues; nothing has changed

industries.industry: Community oncology practices and other Part B drug providers
industries.note: They keep the 6% add-on on the higher average sales price for negotiated drugs, revenue current law would shrink as negotiated prices phase in. Patients also come out ahead on coinsurance, so the provider interest and the patient interest point the same way in this bill.

Net revenue is roughly unchanged — the rebate claws back the difference between the old and negotiated prices — but they avoid selling at the negotiated price directly, and the market benchmark stays at the higher average sales price. They bear the rebate compliance burden.

industries.industry: Medicare (taxpayers and the Part B trust fund)
industries.note: Rebates are deposited into the trust fund, so the negotiated savings continue to flow to Medicare, offsetting the higher provider payments.

analysis.trajectory: With no action in either committee for months and jurisdiction split between two committees, the bill is unlikely to move on its own; most referred bills never get a vote. Its realistic path is being folded into a broader Medicare package if provider groups keep pressing the issue, or expiring at the end of this Congress.
